stages.title: Advanced human physiology
stages.hook: Your blood pressure holds steady as you stand up, run or sleep. Which feedback loops keep the pressure and the acidity of your blood so tightly controlled?
explain: Physiology rests on negative feedback loops: a sensor detects a change, a control centre compares it with a set point, and an effector acts to reverse the change. Blood pressure is monitored by baroreceptors in the carotid arteries and aorta. If pressure falls on standing, the brainstem raises heart rate and narrows blood vessels; if it rises, the opposite happens. Over hours to days, the kidneys also regulate blood volume, aided by hormones such as renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone.

Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is roughly diastolic pressure + one third of the pulse pressure (systolic minus diastolic), and reflects the average driving pressure for blood flow to organs. Perfusion of organs needs an adequate MAP, usually above about 65 mmHg.

Blood acidity is held in a narrow range: arterial pH 7.35 to 7.45. Buffers in the blood act within seconds, the lungs adjust carbon dioxide within minutes (breathing faster removes CO₂ and raises pH), and the kidneys adjust bicarbonate over hours to days. Typical adult arterial values used here: PaCO₂ 35 to 45 mmHg and bicarbonate 22 to 26 mmol/L.

example.q: A fictional adult has a heart rate of 70 beats/min and a stroke volume of 70 mL. What is the cardiac output in L/min?
steps: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
70 × 70 mL = 4900 mL per minute.
Convert: 4900 mL = 4.9 L.

analogies.home: A thermostat compares room temperature with the set point and switches heating on or off.
analogies.city: Water towers and pumps keep pressure steady while use changes through the day.
analogies.tech: A cruise control compares speed with the target and adjusts the engine.
analogies.sea: A ship's ballast tanks fill or empty to keep the ship level.

stages.mnemonic: Sensor, set point, effector: S-S-E. Pressure = flow × resistance.
terms: A loop in which a change triggers a response that reverses the change.
Heart rate × stroke volume, the volume pumped per minute.
The average pressure driving blood to organs.
A pressure sensor in the arteries that tells the brain about blood pressure.
A chemical system that resists changes in pH.

misc.wrong: The body keeps every variable at exactly the same value all the time.
misc.right: Variables fluctuate around a set point or normal range, and set points can shift in states such as exercise, fever or sleep.

stages.limits: Normal values and thresholds differ with age, sex, altitude and disease, and simplified formulae such as MAP are approximations. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

trip.prompt: Trace how a fall in blood pressure leads to a faster heart rate.

questions.q: A fictional adult has a heart rate of 80 beats/min and a stroke volume of 75 mL. What is the cardiac output in L/min?
Blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg. Using MAP = diastolic + one third of (systolic minus diastolic), what is the MAP, to the nearest mmHg?
questions.why: Pulse pressure = 40; one third ≈ 13.3; 80 + 13.3 ≈ 93 mmHg.

questions.q: On standing, blood pools in the legs and pressure briefly falls. What does the baroreflex do?
o: Raises heart rate and narrows vessels
Lowers heart rate and widens vessels
Stops breathing to save oxygen
Makes the kidneys stop working at once
questions.why: The reflex restores pressure to the brain.

questions.q: A negative feedback loop...
o: Reverses a change to restore the set point
Amplifies a change until it grows very large
Is found only in the brain
Never occurs in the human body
questions.why: It opposes the deviation.

questions.q: What is the normal arterial pH range?
o: 6.0 to 6.5, slightly acidic
7.8 to 8.2, slightly alkaline
5.0 to 5.5, like the skin surface
questions.why: Blood is slightly alkaline and tightly controlled.

o: CO₂ falls and pH rises
CO₂ rises and pH falls
Both fall
Both stay fixed
questions.why: Over-breathing blows off CO₂, making blood more alkaline.

questions.q: Order the negative feedback loop for a rise in blood pressure.
items: Brainstem lowers heart rate and widens vessels
questions.why: Sensor, control centre, effector, correction.

questions.q: Match the system to its role in acid-base balance.
pairs: Adjust bicarbonate over hours to days
questions.why: Three layers of control with different speeds.

questions.q: A fictional patient with severe bleeding has a pulse of 130 and a falling blood pressure. Why is the pulse fast?
o: Reflex attempt to maintain cardiac output with less volume
The heart is resting and slow
It is a normal sleep effect
Blood has become thicker and slower
questions.why: Lower stroke volume is compensated by a faster rate until compensation fails.

questions.q: Explain why a fast heart rate in a bleeding patient can be an early warning sign even if blood pressure is still normal.
questions.model: The body compensates for blood loss by raising the heart rate and narrowing vessels, which holds blood pressure up for a while, so tachycardia can appear before pressure falls.
questions.why: Compensation hides early shock.

panel.q: A fictional patient takes medicine that blocks the baroreflex response and feels faint on standing. What explains this?
o: The reflex cannot raise heart rate and tone to correct the drop
The kidneys fail instantly on standing
Blood becomes more acidic at once
Leg muscles stop pumping blood back to the heart
panel.why: Postural hypotension can result when compensation is blunted.

panel.q: A person with severe chronic lung disease has high CO₂ and normal pH over weeks. What explains the normal pH?
o: The kidneys have retained bicarbonate to compensate
The lungs have become healthy again
CO₂ is not acidic at all
The body cannot tolerate pH changes so ignores them
panel.why: Renal compensation is slow and brings pH back toward normal.

panel.q: Why does the body use both fast and slow control mechanisms for blood pressure and acidity?
panel.model: Fast reflexes and buffers prevent immediate danger, while slower kidney and hormonal mechanisms correct sustained disturbances, so the two together give both speed and long-term accuracy.
panel.why: Layered control improves safety.

teach.model: The body keeps variables in a narrow range using negative feedback: a sensor detects change and an effector reverses it. Blood pressure is controlled by quick reflexes and by the kidneys over longer times. Blood pH is controlled by buffers, the lungs and the kidneys.

points.ask: How is blood pressure controlled quickly?

stages.title: Internal medicine
stages.hook: An older patient arrives with tiredness, a mild fever, a new cough and swollen ankles. Could one illness explain all of it?
explain: Internal medicine looks after adults with complex, often multiple, conditions. Physicians combine the history, examination and tests and consider how conditions interact. A patient may have heart failure, diabetes and kidney disease at once, and a treatment for one may affect the others.

Common chronic conditions include hypertension, type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, asthma and COPD. Long-term care emphasises prevention, regular review, risk-factor control (smoking, diet, activity, blood pressure, glucose, cholesterol), vaccination and education. Medicines are reviewed regularly to avoid harm from polypharmacy.

Reasoning starts with the presenting problem, then asks what is the most dangerous cause, what is the most likely cause and what could explain several findings together. Frailty, memory problems and social situation change the best plan. Shared decision making with the patient is central: the aim is what matters to the person, which is not always the longest list of treatments.

example.q: A fictional older adult has breathlessness lying flat, swollen ankles and tiredness. What diagnosis comes to mind and how would a clinician test the idea?
steps: Orthopnoea and leg swelling suggest fluid retention from heart failure.
Examination: raised neck veins, crackles at lung bases, swollen ankles.
Tests: blood tests (including a natriuretic peptide), ECG, chest X-ray and echocardiography.
example.a: Possible heart failure; confirm with examination, blood tests, ECG, chest X-ray and echocardiography

analogies.home: A house may have problems in plumbing and wiring at once; fixing one can affect the other.
analogies.city: Traffic, water and power depend on each other; changing one affects the rest.
analogies.farm: A vet considers feed, water and housing together in a sick herd.
analogies.tech: A system with several linked faults needs a whole-system view.

stages.mnemonic: Think common, dangerous and linked: one illness or several?
terms: Having more than one health condition at once.
Taking many medicines, increasing risk of side effects and interactions.
Reduced reserve making a person vulnerable to stress.

misc.wrong: Every symptom must be explained by a single diagnosis.
misc.right: Older and multi-morbid patients often have several contributing conditions, and medicines themselves may cause symptoms.

stages.limits: Case summaries are simplified. Real diagnosis needs full assessment, and local guidelines set thresholds for treatment. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

panel.model: Chronic conditions and ageing often coexist, so treatments for one may affect another, which means clinicians must review the whole patient and balance benefits and harms.
panel.why: Whole-person care.

teach.topic: Looking after adults with several conditions
teach.model: Internal medicine cares for adults with complex or multiple illnesses. Doctors consider which conditions are likely and dangerous, how treatments interact and what matters to the patient. Regular review prevents harm from too many medicines.

What are the risks of many medicines?
How do plans fit the patient?

stages.title: Paediatrics
stages.hook: Why can't we simply treat a child as a small adult? What changes between a newborn and a teenager?
explain: Children differ from adults in size, physiology, growth and development, and in the way they get ill. Babies have faster heart and breathing rates, a larger head relative to the body, and less reserve, so they can deteriorate quickly. Typical normal resting breathing rate: newborn about 30 to 60 per minute, infant about 25 to 50, young child about 20 to 30, older child about 15 to 25 (approximate). Normal ranges change with age, so clinicians use age-based charts.

Development moves through predictable stages: motor (sitting, walking), language, social and thinking skills. Growth is plotted on centile charts; the pattern over time matters more than a single point. Vaccination schedules protect children from serious infections.

Red flags in an unwell child include a very drowsy or floppy child, difficulty breathing, a fever in a baby under three months (needs urgent assessment), signs of dehydration (sunken soft spot, dry mouth, few wet nappies), a non-blanching rash with fever, and persistent vomiting. Parents' worries are important data. Children should be spoken to age-appropriately, and safeguarding concerns must be reported to the proper team. All cases here are fictional.

example.q: A fictional 6-week-old baby has a fever and is feeding poorly and sleepy. How urgent is this?
steps: Fever in a young infant is a red flag because serious bacterial infection is possible.
Poor feeding and drowsiness add to concern.
This needs urgent senior assessment and tests.
example.a: Urgent: fever in a very young infant with poor feeding needs senior assessment

analogies.home: Small cups hold less; a spill is a bigger fraction of the cup. Small bodies have less reserve.
analogies.nature: A sapling reacts faster to drought than an old tree.
analogies.sport: Training plans are age-matched; a child is not a small adult athlete.
analogies.city: A narrow lane blocks faster than a wide road, as small airways do.

stages.mnemonic: Children are not small adults: age-based norms, fast change, listen to parents.
terms: A chart comparing a child's growth with others of the same age.
A skill typically gained at a certain age, such as walking.
A deficit of body water, which is more dangerous in small children.
Protecting children from harm and neglect.

misc.wrong: A child who is smiling cannot be seriously ill.
misc.right: Children can look well and then deteriorate quickly. Observations, age-based norms and parents' concerns all matter.

stages.limits: Values here are approximate and clinical guidelines use finer age bands. Development varies and wide normal ranges exist. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

Lower in babies than in adults

Ignore the parent and trust the chart alone

o: Follow safeguarding procedures and involve senior colleagues

questions.q: Explain why children's vital sign ranges must be age-specific.
questions.model: Heart and breathing rates are higher in young children and fall as they grow, so adult values would label normal children abnormal and could hide illness in others.
questions.why: Age-appropriate norms prevent errors.

Shame the parent for being misled

o: Respect confidentiality and involve them in decisions, within law and safety limits
Tell everyone about the problem
Ignore the teenager's request
Only ever speak to the parents
panel.why: Adolescents' views and privacy matter, with safeguarding exceptions.

panel.q: Why is it important to record height and weight over time in children?
panel.model: Plotting growth over time shows the trend, so a child who is dropping across centiles can be spotted early and investigated for illness or nutrition problems.
panel.why: Growth is a sensitive indicator of health.

teach.model: Children are not small adults. Their normal heart and breathing rates are higher, they have less reserve and can become ill quickly. Doctors use age-based charts, listen to parents and watch for red flags such as fever in a very young baby.

stages.title: Obstetrics and gynaecology
stages.hook: Pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks and changes almost every system of the mother's body. How does a care team keep both mother and baby safe?
explain: Obstetrics is the care of pregnancy, birth and the period after it; gynaecology is the care of the female reproductive system across life. A typical pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks from the last menstrual period and is divided into three trimesters. Antenatal care checks the mother's blood pressure, urine, weight, blood tests and the baby's growth and wellbeing, and offers vaccines and advice on nutrition, folic acid and warning signs.

The mother's body adapts: blood volume rises by about 40 to 50 percent, heart rate rises, the kidneys filter more, and hormones change. Blood pressure usually dips in mid-pregnancy. Common conditions include anaemia, nausea, gestational diabetes and high blood pressure. Pre-eclampsia, new high blood pressure with other signs such as protein in the urine after 20 weeks, can threaten both mother and baby and needs prompt specialist care.

Warning signs that need urgent assessment include heavy vaginal bleeding, severe headache with visual disturbance, severe abdominal pain, a sudden reduction in the baby's movements, fits, and fever with severe illness. Respectful, culturally sensitive, confidential care and informed choice are central. Skilled attendance at birth and access to emergency care greatly reduce maternal and newborn deaths worldwide. All cases here are fictional.

example.q: A fictional pregnant woman at 34 weeks has a severe headache, blurred vision and blood pressure of 165/110. What should the junior do?
steps: New high blood pressure with severe headache and visual symptoms in late pregnancy suggests severe pre-eclampsia.
It is an emergency that can lead to fits and harm to mother and baby.
Call for senior obstetric help immediately.
example.a: Treat as an obstetric emergency and call senior help immediately

analogies.home: A house under extension needs extra supports and regular checks.
analogies.city: A growing city needs more water, power and roads, like the extra blood volume in pregnancy.
analogies.nature: A seed needs steady soil and water to grow.
analogies.sea: A ship carrying passengers needs extra checks and a skilled crew.

A pregnancy condition with new high blood pressure and other signs, which can be dangerous.

misc.wrong: A healthy pregnancy needs no checks.
misc.right: Antenatal care detects problems such as high blood pressure and anaemia early, when they can be managed.

stages.limits: Care patterns differ across countries and cultures, and this stage gives only a clinical overview with fictional examples. This is not medical advice.

questions.q: Explain why skilled attendance at birth and emergency care reduce maternal deaths.
questions.model: Trained attendants recognise and treat complications such as heavy bleeding or high blood pressure quickly, and access to emergency care means problems are managed before they become fatal.

o: Explain benefits, limits and options, and support her choice

panel.q: Why is pre-eclampsia dangerous to both mother and baby?

panel.why: Multi-system risks.

teach.model: Antenatal care checks the mother's blood pressure, blood and the baby's growth so problems are found early. Warning signs such as heavy bleeding, severe headache with visual problems or reduced baby movements need urgent help. Respectful, skilled care saves lives.

stages.title: Neurology and psychiatry
stages.hook: A person suddenly cannot speak clearly. Another feels sad for months and cannot enjoy anything. Both involve the brain, so how do the specialties differ?
explain: Neurology deals with diseases of the nervous system: stroke, epilepsy, migraine, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, dementia and nerve and muscle disorders. A neurological examination checks consciousness, speech, cranial nerves, strength, sensation, reflexes and coordination. Localising the lesion ('where is the problem?') comes before the question 'what is it?'.

Stroke may be due to a blocked brain artery (ischaemic) or bleeding (haemorrhagic). Time matters because brain tissue is lost each minute. Imaging (usually CT) is needed before some treatments. A seizure is a burst of abnormal electrical activity; first aid is protecting the person from injury, timing the event and calling for help if it lasts more than about five minutes.

Psychiatry deals with mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder and psychosis. Assessment includes mood, thoughts, behaviour, sleep, appetite, functioning and risk to self or others. Clinicians ask directly and kindly about safety, without judgement, and escalate to a senior or crisis team when someone may be at risk. Mental illnesses are medical conditions; stigma delays help. Treatment may combine talking therapies, medicines, social support and lifestyle. All cases here are fictional.

example.q: A fictional adult has sudden left arm weakness and slurred speech that began 45 minutes ago. What is the priority?
steps: This suggests a stroke (FAST positive).
Time is critical, so activate emergency pathways and note the time of onset.
Urgent brain imaging decides between clot and bleeding and guides treatment.
example.a: Activate the stroke pathway, record onset time and get urgent brain imaging

analogies.home: A broken light could be the bulb, wiring or the fuse; neurologists localise the fault.
analogies.tech: A network problem might be in the cable, router or server.
analogies.music: A choir off-key could be one singer or the whole group; mood and thought disorders affect the whole performance.
analogies.nature: A river can be blocked by a dam or burst a bank, like a clot or a bleed.

stages.mnemonic: Neurology: where is the lesion? Psychiatry: how is the person functioning, and are they safe?
terms: A damaged or abnormal area of tissue.
A stroke caused by a blocked brain artery.
A sudden burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain.
A mood disorder with persistent low mood, loss of interest and reduced functioning.
A state in which a person loses contact with shared reality, for example by hearing voices.

misc.wrong: Mental health problems are a personal weakness.
misc.right: They are health conditions with biological, psychological and social causes, and they respond to treatment and support.

stages.limits: This overview simplifies many disorders. Diagnosis and treatment need trained clinicians, and anyone worried about their own safety should contact local emergency or crisis services. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

questions.model: Stigma makes people ashamed, so they delay or avoid seeking help and their condition can worsen; reducing stigma helps people get care sooner.

panel.why: Organic causes of confusion must be excluded.

panel.q: Explain how a clinician balances respect for a patient's wishes with safety when the patient may be at risk.
panel.model: The clinician listens and involves the person in choices while assessing risk, and if there is serious risk or lack of capacity they involve seniors and follow the law to keep the person safe.
panel.why: Autonomy and protection must be balanced.

teach.model: Neurology studies diseases of the brain, nerves and muscles, such as stroke and epilepsy. Stroke is an emergency because brain cells die fast. Psychiatry studies mental health conditions such as depression. Clinicians ask kindly about safety and get help early.

points.ask: How should we respond to someone struggling?

stages.title: Surgery and perioperative care concepts
stages.hook: Surgery begins long before the first cut and ends long after the last stitch. What happens before, during and after an operation?
explain: Perioperative care covers the whole surgical journey: preoperative assessment, anaesthesia and surgery, and postoperative recovery. Before an operation, the team confirms the diagnosis, the patient's fitness, medicines (some must be adjusted), allergies, and informed consent. Fasting before anaesthesia reduces the risk of stomach contents entering the lungs.

Anaesthesia makes the operation painless and safe: general anaesthesia produces unconsciousness; regional or local anaesthesia numbs part of the body. The anaesthetist monitors breathing, heart rate, oxygen, blood pressure and temperature throughout. Surgical safety checklists, such as confirming the right patient, right procedure and right site, and counting instruments, reduce errors.

After surgery, teams control pain, watch for complications (bleeding, infection, clots, breathing problems), encourage early movement and nutrition, and plan discharge. Infection prevention uses clean hands, sterile technique, and sometimes antibiotics given before the operation for selected operations. Not every problem needs surgery; the decision weighs benefit, risk and the patient's wishes, and emergency surgery follows different time pressures.

example.q: A fictional patient the day after an abdominal operation has a rising pulse, falling blood pressure and a swollen, tender abdomen. What is the concern and the action?
steps: Rising pulse and falling BP after surgery suggest bleeding or sepsis.
A swollen, tender abdomen adds to concern.
This is an emergency; do ABCDE and call the surgical senior immediately.
example.a: Possible postoperative bleeding or sepsis; assess ABCDE and call senior help immediately

analogies.home: Building work needs planning, safe tools and tidying afterwards.
analogies.sea: A ship leaves port after checks and is monitored throughout the voyage.
analogies.tech: A software update involves a backup, careful install and testing afterwards.
analogies.sport: A match has a warm-up, the game and a cool-down.

stages.mnemonic: Before, During, After: plan, protect, recover. Right patient, right site, right procedure.
terms: Before, during and after an operation.
Medical control of pain and consciousness for a procedure.
A team checklist to prevent errors such as wrong-site surgery.
A problem arising after surgery, such as bleeding or infection.

misc.wrong: The surgeon alone ensures a safe operation.
misc.right: Safe surgery depends on a team of surgeons, anaesthetists, nurses, theatre staff and checklists.

stages.limits: Practice varies between hospitals and operations. This stage covers concepts only and gives no operative instructions or drug regimens. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

trip.prompt: Find the three phases of the checklist and what is confirmed in each.

questions.q: Perioperative care covers...
o: Before, during and after surgery
Only the operation itself
Only the recovery on the ward
Only the paperwork around surgery
questions.why: The whole surgical pathway.

questions.q: Why is fasting required before general anaesthesia?
o: To reduce the risk of stomach contents entering the lungs
To make the patient lighter for the surgeon
To avoid noise from the stomach
To help the stitches heal neatly
questions.why: Reflexes are reduced during anaesthesia.

questions.q: A surgical safety checklist is used to...
o: Prevent errors such as wrong patient or wrong site
Replace the surgeon's judgement
Replace the need for consent
Save time and nothing else
questions.why: It helps the team catch errors.

questions.q: Which is a postoperative complication?
o: Wound infection
Good appetite on day two
Normal sleep through the night
A healthy pulse and colour
questions.why: Infection, bleeding, clots and breathing problems are possible.

questions.q: Order the perioperative pathway.
questions.why: The standard sequence.

questions.q: Match the team member to a role.
pairs: Keeps the patient asleep and monitored
questions.why: Teamwork is essential.

questions.q: Why encourage early movement after many operations?
o: It helps prevent clots and chest infections
It prevents hunger on the ward
It stops the wound healing
It is a punishment for staying in bed too long
questions.why: Inactivity increases clot and lung risks.

questions.q: A fictional patient taking a blood-thinning medicine needs surgery. What is sensible?
o: Review the medicine plan with the surgical and medical teams in advance
Ignore the medicine and operate as planned
Stop all the patient's medicines without advice
Operate regardless of the bleeding risk
questions.why: Medicines affect bleeding and must be planned.

questions.q: A nurse notices the consent form lists a different side from the planned operation. What should she do?
o: Stop and check with the team before proceeding
Say nothing and assume it will be fixed
Continue quietly with the preparation
Change the form secretly so that it matches the plan
questions.why: Anyone may stop the line to prevent wrong-site surgery.

questions.q: Why does a surgical decision involve weighing benefit and risk with the patient?
questions.model: Surgery can bring benefit but carries risks such as bleeding and infection, so the patient needs enough information to weigh these against their own goals and give informed consent.
questions.why: Informed consent and shared decisions.

panel.q: A frail older person has a problem that might be treated surgically or conservatively. What is the right approach?
o: Discuss options, risks and goals with the patient and team
Always operate whatever the risks
Never operate on a frail person
Decide only by the patient's age
panel.why: Individualised decisions balance risk and goals.

panel.q: A junior notices an instrument count is incorrect at the end of an operation. What is correct?
o: Speak up so it is resolved before closing
Assume it is fine and carry on with closing up
Wait until next week to mention it
Hide the problem to avoid trouble
panel.why: Retained items are a never-event preventable by counts.

panel.q: Why is emergency surgery riskier than planned surgery?
panel.model: In an emergency there is little time to prepare, and patients are often already very unwell, so there are higher chances of complications.
panel.why: Less optimisation raises risk.

teach.model: Perioperative care is the care before, during and after an operation. The team checks the patient is fit and consents, anaesthesia keeps the patient asleep and monitored, and after surgery they watch for complications. Safety checklists prevent errors.

points.ask: What do we watch for afterwards?

stages.title: Cardiology and pulmonology
stages.hook: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity as a wavy line. What can a few small bumps tell a doctor about the whole heart?
explain: The heart's rhythm starts in the sinoatrial (SA) node, spreads through the atria, pauses at the atrioventricular (AV) node and then spreads to the ventricles. On an ECG the P wave shows atrial activation, the QRS complex shows ventricular activation and the T wave shows ventricular recovery. The time between beats on the trace gives the heart rate; for example, a rate of 60 per minute means one beat every second.

Common cardiac problems include coronary artery disease (angina and heart attack), heart failure (the heart cannot pump enough for the body's needs), arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation (irregular rhythm that raises stroke risk), and valve disease. Treatments combine medicines, procedures to open or bypass blocked arteries, devices such as pacemakers, and risk-factor control.

Pulmonology: asthma has reversible airway narrowing, COPD has persistent airflow limitation mostly from smoking, and pneumonia is lung infection. Spirometry measures how much and how fast air can be blown out; in obstructive disease the ratio of FEV₁ to FVC is reduced (below about 0.7). A pulmonary embolism is a clot in the lung arteries and causes sudden breathlessness or chest pain; it is an emergency. Oxygen is given to treat low oxygen levels, with care in some chronic lung disease.

example.q: A fictional patient's FEV₁ is 1.8 L and FVC is 3.0 L. What is the FEV₁/FVC ratio, and what does it suggest?
steps: A ratio below about 0.7 suggests airflow obstruction.
Together with the history, it suggests COPD or asthma; reversibility testing helps tell them apart.

analogies.music: An ECG is like sheet music for the heart's rhythm: a rhythm out of time suggests an arrhythmia.
analogies.city: The SA node is like a traffic signal that sets the pace.
analogies.home: A pump with a leaking valve wastes energy.
analogies.nature: Asthma is like a narrowed stream; COPD is like a permanently silted channel.

stages.mnemonic: P for atria, QRS for ventricles, T for recovery. FEV₁/FVC below 0.7 means obstruction.
terms: An irregular, often fast rhythm from the atria that raises stroke risk.
A test measuring how much and how fast air can be blown out.
A clot blocking an artery in the lungs.

misc.wrong: An ECG shows how well the heart pumps.
misc.right: An ECG shows the heart's electrical activity; pump function is assessed by imaging such as echocardiography.

stages.limits: ECG and spirometry interpretation needs context and training. Thresholds are guideline-based and vary slightly. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

trip.prompt: Locate the P wave, QRS complex and T wave on a normal trace.

questions.q: On an ECG, the QRS complex represents...
o: Ventricular activation
Atrial activation
The volume of the lungs
The patient's breathing pattern
questions.why: P = atria, QRS = ventricles, T = recovery.

questions.q: What is the heart's natural pacemaker?
o: Sinoatrial node
The aortic valve
The left lung
The diaphragm
questions.why: The SA node sets the rhythm.

questions.q: FEV₁ is 2.4 L and FVC is 4.0 L. What is the FEV₁/FVC ratio?
A ratio of 0.6 on spirometry in an adult most suggests...
o: Obstructive airway disease
Normal lungs in a healthy adult
A heart attack in progress
Anaemia from low iron
questions.why: Below about 0.7 suggests obstruction.

questions.q: Why does atrial fibrillation raise stroke risk?
o: Blood can pool and form clots in the atria which may travel to the brain
It slows the brain's own signals
It dilates the lungs' airways
It lowers glucose in the blood
questions.why: Clots may embolise.

questions.q: Match the condition to its key feature.
pairs: Heart cannot meet the body's needs
questions.why: Core features.

questions.q: A fictional patient has sudden breathlessness and sharp chest pain after a long period in bed. What must be considered?
o: Pulmonary embolism, which is an emergency
Hay fever from pollen
Indigestion only, needing a simple antacid
Dehydration from too little water
questions.why: Immobility is a risk factor for clots.

questions.q: Order the spread of the heartbeat signal.
questions.why: The delay lets ventricles fill.

questions.q: A fictional patient with long-standing COPD and very high CO₂ is given a lot of oxygen. Why take care?
o: In some patients, too much oxygen can reduce the drive to breathe and raise CO₂ further
Oxygen is always harmful to every patient
Oxygen causes a high fever
No care is needed with oxygen in any patient
questions.why: Target oxygen levels are set carefully for those at risk of CO₂ retention.

questions.q: Explain why an ECG alone cannot show how strongly the heart is pumping.
questions.model: An ECG records electrical activity and rhythm, not the mechanical pumping, so pump function is assessed with imaging such as an echocardiogram.
questions.why: Electrical and mechanical function differ.

panel.q: A fictional patient with an irregular pulse and palpitations is otherwise well. Which approach is sensible?
o: Record an ECG, assess stroke risk and involve a senior
Ignore it as it is probably nothing
Reassure and discharge without any tests
Treat it as asthma with an inhaler
panel.why: Possible atrial fibrillation needs rhythm confirmation and stroke prevention planning.

panel.q: A well-controlled asthmatic uses a reliever more and more each week. What does this suggest?
o: Worsening control that needs review
Better control than before
No change in control
The asthma has been cured
panel.why: Increasing reliever use signals poor control.

panel.q: Explain the difference between asthma and COPD in terms of reversibility and cause.
panel.model: Asthma has airway narrowing that is variable and largely reversible, often with allergic triggers, while COPD has persistent, progressive airflow limitation usually linked to smoking or other long-term exposures.
panel.why: Reversibility and cause differ.

teach.topic: The heart's rhythm and the lungs' airflow
teach.model: The heart's pacemaker, the SA node, starts each beat, and an ECG records this electrical signal. Spirometry measures airflow, and a low FEV₁/FVC ratio shows obstruction as in asthma or COPD. Sudden breathlessness with chest pain can be a clot in the lungs, which is an emergency.

points.ask: How do asthma and COPD differ?

stages.title: Nephrology, endocrinology and gastroenterology
stages.hook: A patient has high blood sugar, swollen ankles and abdominal pain after meals. Which organs link these problems?
explain: Nephrology: the kidneys filter blood; the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) estimates filtering ability. A normal eGFR is above about 90 mL/min/1.73 m²; chronic kidney disease is defined by reduced eGFR or kidney damage lasting more than three months. Causes include diabetes and high blood pressure. Acute kidney injury is a sudden fall in function, often in the context of illness, dehydration or medicines, and needs prompt recognition. Dangerous consequences include high potassium and fluid overload.

Endocrinology: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune loss of insulin-making cells; type 2 involves insulin resistance and reduced insulin production. Diagnosis uses blood glucose or HbA1c; HbA1c reflects average glucose over about 2 to 3 months, with 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or higher a diagnostic threshold when confirmed. Diabetic ketoacidosis, an emergency in which a lack of insulin leads to acid build-up, shows with thirst, vomiting, fast deep breathing and drowsiness. Thyroid disease can speed up (overactive) or slow down (underactive) metabolism.

Gastroenterology: common problems are reflux, peptic ulcer, inflammatory bowel disease, gallstones, hepatitis and cirrhosis. Red flags include vomiting blood, black tarry stools, trouble swallowing, unexplained weight loss, jaundice (yellow skin and eyes) and severe constant abdominal pain. Liver tests and ultrasound help to separate liver from gallbladder or blockage causes.

example.q: A fictional person with type 1 diabetes has vomiting, fast deep breathing and drowsiness. Their blood glucose is very high. What is the concern?
steps: Type 1 diabetes with vomiting, fast deep breathing and drowsiness suggests diabetic ketoacidosis.
It is a medical emergency with acid build-up and dehydration.
Call senior help urgently and start the emergency protocol.
example.a: Diabetic ketoacidosis: an emergency needing urgent senior help

analogies.home: A filter in a water system clogs over time, like a kidney with reduced eGFR.
analogies.farm: A farmer's pump needs the right fuel (insulin) to move water (glucose) into the fields (cells).
analogies.city: A water treatment works, a power regulator and a food processing plant must all keep running.
analogies.tech: A thermostat that is stuck high or low is like an overactive or underactive thyroid.

stages.mnemonic: Kidney: filter and balance. Endocrine: hormones and glucose. Gut: digest and detox via the liver.
terms: An estimate of how well the kidneys filter blood.
A blood test reflecting average glucose over about 2 to 3 months.
A dangerous acid build-up in diabetes from lack of insulin.
Yellow colouring of the skin and eyes from raised bilirubin.

misc.wrong: Type 2 diabetes is only about eating sugar.
misc.right: It results from insulin resistance and reduced insulin production, influenced by genes, weight, activity and other factors.

stages.limits: Thresholds and treatments vary by guideline and patient, and there are many types of kidney, hormone and gut disease not covered here. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

o: How well the kidneys filter blood
How fast the heart beats
The level of blood sugar
The capacity of the lungs

questions.q: HbA1c reflects...
o: Average blood glucose over about 2 to 3 months
The meal eaten earlier today
Blood pressure over a week
The rhythm of the heart
questions.why: Glycated haemoglobin.

questions.q: Which is a red flag in the gut?
o: Vomiting blood
Mild hunger
Occasional burping
A good appetite
questions.why: May signal upper GI bleeding.

questions.q: Yellow skin and eyes (jaundice) suggest...
o: Raised bilirubin from liver, gallbladder or blood problems
An excess of vitamin D
Hay fever or an allergy
A fracture of a long bone
questions.why: Bilirubin builds up.

questions.q: Match the condition to its main feature.
questions.why: Key mechanisms.

questions.q: A fictional patient taking an anti-inflammatory painkiller, dehydrated from a stomach bug, passes very little urine. What should be considered?
o: Acute kidney injury
Perfect kidney function
Excess insulin
Normal ageing
questions.why: Dehydration and some medicines can cause AKI.

questions.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a potassium of 6.5 mmol/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0). What is the concern?
o: Risk of dangerous heart rhythm problems needing urgent attention
Nothing to worry about
A normal result for kidney disease
A dangerously low blood sugar
questions.why: Severe hyperkalaemia is an emergency.

questions.q: Order the typical path to diagnosing diabetes in an unwell fictional adult.
items: Symptoms: thirst and passing a lot of urine
HbA1c or repeat test to confirm
questions.why: Suspect, test, confirm, plan.

questions.q: A diagnostic HbA1c threshold for diabetes is 48 mmol/mol. A fictional patient has 53 mmol/mol. By how many mmol/mol does it exceed the threshold?
Explain why high blood pressure and diabetes can damage the kidneys.
questions.model: Over years, high pressure and high glucose damage the tiny blood vessels and filters in the kidneys, causing scarring and a gradual loss of function.
questions.why: Microvascular damage.

panel.q: A fictional patient with a long history of heavy alcohol use has jaundice, a swollen abdomen and confusion. What is the concern?
o: Advanced liver disease needing urgent assessment
A mild cold with a cough
Hay fever in the summer
A muscle strain from lifting
panel.why: Cirrhosis with complications.

panel.q: A person with diabetes avoids insulin because of fear of needles. What is the best approach?
o: Explore the fear, offer support and explain options
Withhold care until they accept insulin
Shame them for being afraid
Ignore the fear and move on
panel.why: Empathy and education improve adherence.

panel.q: Why is a sudden reduction in urine output after surgery or illness important to report?
panel.model: Falling urine output can be an early sign that the kidneys are not getting enough blood flow or are injured, so early reporting allows treatment before lasting damage.
panel.why: Urine output is a sensitive sign.

teach.model: The kidneys filter blood, and eGFR shows how well. Diabetes is a problem with insulin that raises blood glucose, and ketoacidosis is an emergency. The gut and liver digest food; vomiting blood, black stools or jaundice are warning signs.

stages.title: Evidence-based clinical decision-making
stages.hook: A new treatment helps in a study, but the study had only twelve people and no comparison group. Should a hospital adopt it tomorrow?
explain: Evidence-based medicine combines the best available research with clinical expertise and the patient's values. Studies sit on a hierarchy: systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised trials give the strongest evidence for treatments, then single randomised controlled trials, cohort and case-control studies, case series and expert opinion. Randomisation reduces confounding by balancing known and unknown factors between groups, and blinding reduces bias.

Key measures: absolute risk reduction (ARR) is the difference in event rates between groups; relative risk reduction (RRR) is ARR divided by the control risk; number needed to treat (NNT) = 1 ÷ ARR. A treatment with a big relative reduction may still help few people if the baseline risk is low. Confidence intervals show the precision of an estimate, and a p-value is the probability of seeing results at least this extreme if there were truly no effect; it does not measure the importance of an effect.

Appraise: Is the question clear? Were participants similar and allocated fairly? Were outcomes measured objectively? Were all participants followed up? Are the results precise and relevant to my patient? Also consider harms, cost and fairness, and conflicts of interest. Guidelines summarise evidence but need judgement for the individual patient, especially those underrepresented in trials such as the very old, children and pregnant people.

example.q: In a trial, 10% of the control group and 6% of the treated group have a stroke. What are ARR, RRR and NNT?
steps: RRR = ARR ÷ control risk = 4 ÷ 10 = 40%.

analogies.home: A recipe tested on many kitchens is more reliable than one cook's boast.
analogies.sport: A training method tested across many teams gives better evidence than a single success story.
analogies.city: A new bus route tried in one street may not suit the whole city.
analogies.tech: A software fix tested only on one machine may fail elsewhere.

stages.mnemonic: Question, Evidence, Appraise, Apply, Assess: evidence plus expertise plus patient values.
terms: A study in which participants are randomly allocated to treatment or comparison.
The difference in event risk between control and treated groups.
The number of people who must be treated for one to benefit: 1 ÷ ARR.
A range of values likely to include the true effect.
A mixing of effects that makes a link appear because of a third factor.

misc.wrong: A statistically significant result always means an important treatment effect.
misc.right: Significance depends on sample size; the size of the effect, harms and relevance to the patient also matter.

stages.limits: Evidence quality varies, trials may not include all patient groups, and guidelines may disagree. Judgement and patient preferences remain essential. Patients here are fictional, and this is not medical advice.

trip.prompt: Look at the hierarchy of evidence and find where randomised trials sit.

questions.q: In a trial, 20% of controls and 15% of treated patients have an event. What is the ARR in percentage points?
The ARR is 0.05. What is the NNT?
Control event rate is 10% and treated event rate is 5%. What is the RRR as a percentage?
Which provides the strongest evidence for a treatment effect?
o: A systematic review of randomised trials
A single case report in a medical journal
Expert opinion alone
A patient testimonial online
questions.why: Combining well-conducted RCTs reduces bias and imprecision.

questions.q: Why randomise participants?
o: To balance known and unknown factors between groups
To make the trial last longer
To please the doctors running it
To reduce the sample size needed
questions.why: It reduces confounding.

questions.q: A drug halves a very rare event risk from 2 in 100,000 to 1 in 100,000. What is true?
o: Relative reduction is large but absolute benefit is tiny
There is no benefit at all
The absolute benefit is large
The relative reduction is tiny
questions.why: RRR 50%, ARR 0.001 percentage points.

questions.q: What does blinding in a trial mean?
o: Participants or assessors do not know who gets which treatment
Nobody is allowed to see the final results
The study has no control group at all
The trial is kept secret from regulators
questions.why: Blinding reduces bias in reporting and assessing outcomes.

questions.q: A small study of twelve patients without a control group shows improvement. What is the best conclusion?
o: It is weak evidence and needs better trials
The treatment is now fully proven to work
The treatment is useless
It should be adopted everywhere at once
questions.why: No control and small numbers limit reliability.

questions.q: Order the evidence-based practice steps.
items: Apply it with the patient's values and review the outcome
questions.why: Ask, acquire, appraise, apply, assess.

questions.q: Why do guidelines still need clinical judgement for an individual patient?
questions.model: Guidelines summarise average results from trial populations, but the individual may differ, have other conditions or different preferences, so clinicians adapt recommendations to the person.
questions.why: Evidence informs, not dictates.

panel.q: A company-funded trial reports only its positive outcomes. What is the concern?
o: Reporting and funding bias may overstate benefit
No concern; reports are always complete
It is automatically correct because the company paid for it
The company is itself a doctor
panel.why: Selective reporting and conflicts of interest distort evidence.

panel.q: An observational study finds coffee drinkers live longer. What should you consider before concluding that coffee causes this?
o: Confounding, such as other lifestyle differences
Nothing further needs to be considered
That coffee is itself a drug
That coffee is cheap to buy
panel.why: Association does not prove causation.

panel.q: Explain why NNT and absolute risk are more informative for a patient than relative risk alone.
panel.model: Relative reductions can sound impressive even when the baseline risk is tiny, whereas absolute risk and NNT show how many people actually benefit, helping patients weigh benefits against harms.
panel.why: Absolute numbers give context.

teach.model: Evidence-based medicine combines the best research with a clinician's skill and the patient's values. Randomised trials give strong evidence. Absolute risk and NNT show how much a treatment really helps. Guidelines still need judgement for each patient.

points.ask: How do we see how much it helps?
